canonicalRules: Every page carries an absolute, self-referencing canonical. No page canonicalises to another unless explicitly declared here.
All query parameters are stripped from the canonical. Parameters carry UI state only and never produce different content.
No trailing slash, site-wide. A trailing slash 301s to the slash-free version.
Apex only or www only — pick one, 301 the rest. HTTP always 301s to HTTPS.
Lowercase across the whole path. A path with an uppercase character 301s.
Paginated directory pages each carry their own canonical, not a canonical back to page one.
No page is both canonicalised and noindexed — that is a contradictory signal.
differentiationRules: **The generic/entity rule — the single most important anti-cannibalisation rule:** a generic tool with a location selector is never optimised for an entity-qualified query. `/tools/income-tax-calculator` carries no 'California' in its title, H1, meta or H2; that query belongs to `/state-taxes/california`. And the reverse: a state page is never optimised for the generic keyword.
Directory versus tool: a directory **lists**, a tool **calculates**. A directory never embeds a full calculator, and a tool never renders the full entity list. If both do both, one of them has to go.

The four salary-family tools (income tax / take-home / paycheck / withholding) have genuinely different primary outputs, and that difference must be visible in the H1, the first sentence and the headline number of the ResultCard — not only in the URL.
No page is optimised for a keyword absent from `data/keywords.json`. An unmeasured keyword is an unproven target.
Monthly Search Console review: if two of our URLs take impressions for one query, within that same month one of them changes target or is canonicalised. Delay drags both down.

Affordability and payment are different questions and must produce visibly different headline numbers: /tools/home-affordability-calculator answers 'what is the most I can buy' (a price), /tools/house-payment-calculator answers 'what does this cost me monthly' (a payment). The same separation holds for rent affordability against cost of living.

onPage.$comment: Title/meta/H1 patterns per template, enforced by scripts/audit_seo.py. For 104 programmatic pages these formulas control SERP click-through directly; written once here rather than improvised per page. Everything in this file is English: it feeds the build.

ToolPage.title: {Primary} ({year})
rules: The primary keyword appears **verbatim** in the title and H1 — not a near variant.
The year appears in the title but **never in the URL** (section 6-7).
The meta must state the differentiating output, not a generic description — this is what separates the four salary-family tools from each other.
No generic tool carries an entity name in its title (the generic/entity rule).
The meta comes from each page's `metaHook` — English, 110-155 characters, naming the differentiating output.
The 'how it is calculated' H2 names the **subject**, not the tool: 'How sales tax is calculated', never 'How Sales Tax Calculator is calculated'. Every tool page therefore declares a `subject` field.

PlacePage.title: Cost of Living in {Metro} ({year})
PlacePage.meta: What a month costs in {Metro}, from official BEA and HUD data — rent, goods, services, and what you keep after {State} tax.
rules: The place name appears in the title, the H1, and the first 40 characters of the meta.
The meta references **state tax** — the differentiator competitors lack.

**Formulas use the metro's display name, never its full MSA name.** `San Francisco-Oakland-Berkeley, CA` is 34 characters against `Akron`'s 5, and no single formula fits a 45-character meta window across that range. The full MSA name appears once in the body, where it is a precision signal rather than a layout problem.
**displayName is capped at 20 characters** and is a required field on every metro row. It is the value the audit sizes formulas against.
h2Outline: What it costs to live in {Metro}

StateTaxPage.title: {State} Income Tax Calculator ({year})
StateTaxPage.meta: Estimate {State} state and federal income tax on your salary, with a bracket-by-bracket breakdown of exactly where each dollar goes.
rules: The state name comes first — the user's query is 'california income tax', not 'income tax california'.
The nine no-tax states get a different meta: '{State} has no state income tax — here is what you still owe federally'.

DirectoryPage.title: {Primary} ({year})
rules: A directory never repeats a tool keyword in its title.
Outlines are per page. One outline across three directories is template furniture: a list of cities, a list of states and a list of calculators do not share a structure.

No 'Frequently asked questions' heading. structuredData forbids FAQPage on a directory because a directory lists rather than answers, and an H2 with nothing behind it is thin content whichever way it is marked up.

Home.title: Cost of Living and Take-Home Pay Calculators
Home.h1: What a place really costs — and what you keep
rules: The home page targets no head keyword — it does not compete with its own tools.

TrustPage.title: {Primary} — {SiteName}
rules: Trust pages target no search keyword and are not optimised for one. They exist for AdSense review (10-1), for E-E-A-T (7-4), and for people — and a trust page chasing a keyword reads as exactly the thing it is meant to disprove.
They are **indexed**, never noindex: an About page Google cannot see does not support authority.
They carry **no ads** (rule 10-4-6).
The title is the page's own name — 'Methodology', not 'Methodology | Free Tax Calculator 2026'.

Outlines are per page, not per template: an About page and a Privacy page share no structure, and forcing one outline on both produces headings that are wrong on at least one of them — the same defect found on the no-tax state pages (9-3-9).

The title carries the site name because the page name alone is too short to be a useful SERP line — 'Privacy' is 7 characters. This is the one place a brand suffix is right: the page has no keyword to lose room for.

GuidePage.title: {Primary} ({year})
rules: A guide is 1,500-2,500 words with at least one worked example computed by our own engine, never a hypothetical number (7-2-2).
It links to at least two of our tools in the body, where the reader needs them.
It never embeds a full calculator — that is the directory-versus-tool rule applied to guides (differentiationRules[1]).
Its head term must be measured into data/keywords.json before it is written (plannedPages.promotionRule).

anchorText: Link to an entity page with the **entity name**: 'Cost of Living in Austin' — never 'click here' or 'read more'.
Link to a tool with **that tool's primary keyword**, and never more than once with identical text on the same page.
Anchor text is never the linking page's **own** keyword — an outbound link is written with the destination page's keyword.
Navigation and footer links are exempt from the 25-body-link ceiling but must stay identical across pages.
openGraph: Per-entity OG image — the place name and its index number rendered on the image. If the platform cannot generate images per row, a per-template static image is the fallback; what must never happen is one image for the whole site, because then every shared link looks like every other.
A static image for tools, carrying the tool name.
`og:title` may differ from `<title>` — the year is dropped on social networks.
Without an OG image a link looks dead on Reddit and forums — and section 9-5 earns its links there.

Required tags on every page: og:title, og:description, og:url (the canonical, absolute), og:type, og:image (absolute URL, 1200x630), og:site_name, twitter:card=summary_large_image. A relative og:image is not fetched.
robots: No content page is ever disallowed. If a page is not worth indexing, it is not generated at all.
`Sitemap:` points at `sitemap.xml`, which itself has four child sitemaps (section 6-8-6).
No `crawl-delay` — Google ignores it and it only slows other crawlers.

ToolPage: FAQPage — only when the FAQ is actually visible on the page
PlacePage: Dataset — points at the BEA/HUD source
global: `dateModified` only on a genuine content change (section 9-4-1)
DirectoryPage: ItemList — the table rows, each with its position and link
No FAQPage — a directory lists, it does not answer questions
TrustPage: Organization + Person on /about — this is where the author identity actually lives (7-4)
No FAQPage — a policy page is not a Q&A

headingRules: Exactly one H1 per page, and it is the head term (9-3-2).
No H2 repeats the H1 — a heading that restates the title adds nothing and reads as stuffing.
**Cluster variants belong in H2s, the FAQ and body copy** — this is what makes the page rank for its group rather than only its head (9-2-1).
Headings never skip a level: H1 to H2 to H3, never H1 to H3.
Every template ends with an FAQ H2, because the FAQ is the People Also Ask surface and the FAQPage schema has to have a visible counterpart (9-3-3).
An entity template's outline must name the entity in at least one H2, or every generated page shares an identical outline.
breadcrumbRules: The breadcrumb matches the URL hierarchy and the BreadcrumbList JSON-LD exactly — a mismatch between the two is a structured-data error Google reports.
The final crumb is the current page and is not a link.
'Calculators' is the label for /tools; the crumb label need not equal the slug.

These are the highest-volume pages on the site and had no FAQ at all. NOTE ON RICH RESULTS: since August 2023 Google shows FAQ rich results only for well-known government and health sites, so the FAQPage markup here will not produce them. The value is the on-page content itself — People Also Ask capture and long-tail coverage — not the snippet.
cost-of-living-calculator: How is cost of living calculated?

It is a price level, not a budget. The index used here comes from BEA Regional Price Parities, which measure the price of rent, goods and services in one metro against the national average of 100 — so a metro at 112 is 12% more expensive than the country as a whole.
What is included in cost of living?

Rent, goods and services. Rent comes from HUD Fair Market Rent at county level, and it is the component that varies most between places. Income tax is not part of the price level and is handled separately, because two places at the same price level can leave you with very different amounts of money.
Is cost of living the same as inflation?

No, and confusing the two is the most common error here. Inflation measures how prices change over time in one place; a cost-of-living index measures how prices differ between places at one point in time. CPI cannot tell you whether Austin is cheaper than San Francisco.
What salary do I need in this city?

That is the reverse calculation, and it depends on household size as much as on the city. The living wage calculator solves for the gross salary a place requires rather than the cost a salary has to cover.
rent-affordability-calculator: How much rent can I afford on my salary?

The federal standard is 30% of gross income, which comes from the Brooke Amendment: 25% in 1969, raised to 30% in 1981. A household paying above 30% is officially cost burdened, and above 50% severely cost burdened.

It is a policy threshold, not a market forecast. In the most expensive metros 30% of a median income does not reach the 40th-percentile rent, which is why this tool shows your ceiling next to the metro's actual rent rather than returning the percentage alone.

Most screening uses a gross multiple rather than a percentage: commonly three times the monthly rent in gross monthly income, which works out to a 33% ceiling. New York often uses 40x the monthly rent in annual income. What you can carry and what you will be approved for are different numbers.

HUD publishes rent both with and without a utility allowance, and the gap runs from roughly $80 to over $250 a month depending on climate and unit type. A figure quoted without saying which one it is will be wrong by that much.
cost-of-living-comparison: How do I compare the cost of living between two cities?

Compare price levels, not budgets. Each metro carries a BEA Regional Price Parity against a national base of 100, so the ratio between two metros' figures is the real difference in what a month costs there.
Does a higher salary in an expensive city leave me better off?

Not reliably. The price difference between two metros and the state income tax difference work in the same direction more often than people expect, so a raise that looks large in gross terms can be smaller than the cost gap it has to cover.
Which costs differ most between cities?

Rent, by a wide margin. Goods and services vary far less because they move through national supply chains, which is why a comparison that averages everything together understates how much of the difference is housing.
Is a cost of living comparison the same as a salary comparison?
No. A cost comparison tells you what a place charges; a salary comparison tells you what an income is worth there after tax. Both are needed, and the second is the one job offers usually omit.
salary-to-hourly-calculator: How do I convert a salary to an hourly rate?
Divide the annual salary by the hours worked in a year. A standard full-time year is 2,080 hours — 40 hours over 52 weeks — so $95,000 becomes about $45.67 an hour before tax.

It ignores paid leave. A salaried employee with three weeks off is still paid for 2,080 hours but works closer to 1,960, which raises the effective hourly rate by about 6%. A contractor paid only for hours worked has no such cushion.
How do I convert hourly pay to a salary?
Multiply by the hours you actually work in a year rather than by 2,080. The distinction matters most for part-time and shift work, where the assumed number drives the whole answer.
Should I compare offers by hourly rate or salary?

Neither on its own. An hourly rate ignores benefits and paid leave, and a salary ignores the hours behind it. Comparing what each leaves after tax in the place you would live is the only version that settles the question.
salary-comparison-by-city: How do I compare job offers in two different cities?
Convert both to what they leave after tax, then measure each against what its city charges. An offer is better only if it wins on both, and a gross-to-gross comparison decides neither.
Does a raise cover a move to a more expensive city?

Only if it clears the price gap and the tax gap together. Moving from a state with no income tax to one with a progressive schedule can cost several thousand dollars a year on an identical salary, on top of the higher rent.
Which states have no income tax?
Nine: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington and Wyoming. They are not automatically cheaper — several recover the revenue through sales and property tax.
How much does state tax change take-home pay?
On a $95,000 salary the spread between the best and worst jurisdiction is about $7,167 a year, or 7.5% of the salary. None of it appears in an offer letter.
living-wage-calculator: The gross salary that covers a specific place's actual costs for a specific household. It is computed from local rent, goods, services and tax, unlike a minimum wage, which is a statutory floor set without reference to any of them.
How is a living wage different from the minimum wage?

The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 2009, which is $15,080 over a 2,080-hour year — below the poverty guideline for a household of two in every state. A living wage is an arithmetic result; a minimum wage is a legislated number.
Does a living wage include savings?

No. It is a break-even figure covering costs without debt repayment, retirement saving beyond payroll deductions, or discretionary spending. Knowing how far an offer sits above the floor is a separate and more useful question.
Why does household size change the answer so much?

Child care behaves like a second rent. For a household with two young children it exceeds housing costs in much of the country, which is why the gap between household types is usually larger than the gap between cities.
sales-tax-calculator: How do I calculate sales tax?

Multiply the pre-tax price by the combined rate, which is the state rate plus any county, city and special district rates. The combined rate is what you pay, and it is often well above the state rate alone.
Which states have no sales tax?
Five: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon. Alaska is the exception that matters — it has no state sales tax but permits local ones, so parts of the state do charge it.
Why does the rate change within one state?

Because local jurisdictions stack their own rates on top of the state rate. Two addresses a few miles apart can face different combined rates, which is why a state-level figure is not enough to price a purchase.
Does sales tax affect the cost of living?
Yes, and it is the part most cost-of-living comparisons leave out. A state with no income tax that charges a high combined sales tax recovers much of the difference on everything you buy.
income-tax-calculator: Federal tax is bracketed: each slice of taxable income is taxed at its own rate, so the top rate applies only to the income above that threshold, never to the whole amount. State tax is then applied under that state's own rules.
What is the difference between marginal and effective tax rate?

The marginal rate is what the next dollar is taxed at; the effective rate is total tax divided by total income. The effective rate is always lower, and mistaking one for the other is why people overestimate what a raise costs them.
No. Nine levy no income tax on wages. Of the rest, some apply a single flat rate and others a progressive schedule with a top rate above 10%.
Is income tax the same as what comes out of my paycheck?

No. What is withheld comes from the W-4 on file and is an estimate; the liability calculated here is the actual amount owed for the year. The refund or bill in April is the difference between the two.
take-home-pay-calculator: How do I calculate take-home pay?
Subtract federal income tax, state income tax, Social Security at 6.2% and Medicare at 1.45% from gross pay. Social Security and Medicare together are FICA, 7.65% for an employee.
Why is my take-home pay so much lower than my salary?

On a $95,000 salary the deductions run to roughly a quarter of the figure, and the exact amount depends on the state by as much as $7,167 a year. Pre-tax deductions like a 401(k) and health premiums change it further.
What is the difference between biweekly and semi-monthly pay?

Biweekly is every two weeks: 26 checks a year, with two months containing three of them. Semi-monthly is twice a month: 24 checks of identical size. At the same salary the biweekly check is smaller, and the two extra checks close the gap.

Yes. An employer pays a matching 7.65% FICA that never appears on a payslip. A self-employed person pays both halves — 15.3% — which is the largest single difference between an employee and a contractor at the same gross figure.
property-tax-calculator: Assessed value multiplied by the local rate, often expressed in mills. Assessed value is set by the county and is frequently lower than market value, so applying a rate to a sale price overstates the bill.
Which states have the highest property tax?
New Jersey and Illinois exceed 2% of value a year, while Hawaii sits near 0.3%. On a $1,000,000 home that difference is more than $1,400 a month.
Does property tax affect what I can afford?
Directly. Lenders count it inside the housing ratio, so a high-tax county reduces the price you qualify for at an identical income and interest rate.
Can property tax rise after I buy?
Yes. Reassessment on sale is common, and a bill based on the previous owner's assessment can rise sharply in the first year. Some states cap annual increases; most do not cap the reset at sale.
home-affordability-calculator: How much house can I afford?
Conventional underwriting applies two ratios to gross monthly income: 28% for housing alone and 36% for housing plus all other debt. The second is the binding one for most buyers.

A guideline, not a law. The Qualified Mortgage standard allows debt-to-income up to 43%, FHA lending routinely approves above that, and automated underwriting has pushed some approvals near 50%. The conservative answer and the maximum answer are far apart.
How do car and student loans affect it?

They count fully against the back-end ratio while contributing nothing toward the house. Two households with identical incomes and a $600 monthly difference in car payments qualify for roughly $100,000 of price difference.
Is the price I qualify for the price I should pay?

No. Closing costs run 2% to 5% of the purchase price and are paid at the table, and maintenance is conventionally budgeted at 1% of home value a year. Neither reduces what you qualify for; both reduce what you should want.
closing-cost-calculator: Typically 2% to 5% of the purchase price for a buyer. On a $400,000 home that is $8,000 to $20,000, due at closing and separate from the down payment.
What is included in closing costs?

Lender fees, title insurance, escrow and recording fees, appraisal, prepaid interest, and the first instalments of property tax and homeowners insurance. The prepaid items are the part most estimates leave out.
Who pays closing costs, the buyer or the seller?
Both, in different proportions, and the split is negotiable and varies by state. The seller usually carries the agent commissions; transfer taxes fall on either side depending on local custom.
Why do closing costs vary so much by state?
Transfer taxes and title practice differ sharply. Some states charge no transfer tax at all while others charge above 1% of the price, which alone can double the buyer's total.
house-payment-calculator: What is included in a monthly house payment?

Principal, interest, property tax, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance where the down payment is under 20% — together known as PITI. A figure covering only principal and interest understates the real payment substantially.
What is PMI and when does it stop?

Private mortgage insurance is charged when the down payment falls below 20% of the price. On a conventional loan it can be cancelled once equity reaches 20%, and lenders must remove it automatically at 22%.
How much does the interest rate change the payment?
A great deal over a 30-year term, because early payments are almost entirely interest. The rate also changes the price you qualify for, since lenders test the payment rather than the loan amount.
Is a house payment the same as what a home costs me?
No. Maintenance, conventionally budgeted at 1% of value a year, and HOA dues where they apply sit outside the payment entirely and outside every lender calculation.

h2Variants.$comment: An outline formula that ignores its entity's shape produces headings that are wrong on the page — 'Texas tax brackets' on a state that has none. The generator picks the variant from the dataset's `structure` field.

crawl.$comment: The internal link graph from section 6-10-5, declared so that click depth and orphan pages are computed rather than assumed. A page reachable only from a paginated directory is a page Google crawls late and values low.
crawl.globalNavNote: Present in the header of every page. Exempt from the 25-body-link ceiling, but it is what guarantees no page sits deeper than the directory that lists it.
anchorRules: Anchor text is written with the DESTINATION page's head term, never the source's own keyword — an outbound link that repeats your own target keyword gives the signal to the wrong page.
No generic anchors: 'click here', 'read more', 'learn more', 'this page', 'here'.
No two links on one page share anchor text.
An entity link carries the entity name, so the same template produces a different anchor on every generated page — 'Cost of Living in Austin', not 'this city'.
Navigation anchors are fixed site-wide and are exempt from the per-page uniqueness rule, since they appear on every page by design.
crawl.globalFooterNote: Present in the footer of every page. This is what keeps the trust pages out of orphan status without putting policy links in the main navigation, and it is why they are exempt from the per-page anchor-uniqueness rule.

clusterModel.$comment: A page targets an intent cluster, represented by a head term — not a single keyword string. `primary` is the head; `cluster.variants` are the phrasings the same page is expected to rank for; `cluster.intent` is what they all mean. Intent is the real anti-cannibalisation axis: two pages may be lexically distant and still compete, or lexically close and not.
clusterModel.variantsAreUnmeasured: Variant volumes are NOT measured. They are linguistic expansions of the head term, and they deliberately carry no numbers. Nothing here feeds scripts/model_revenue.py, which continues to compute from measured heads only, so the revenue model stays conservative rather than being inflated by estimates nobody checked. Measure them against real data before using any of them to justify a decision.
rules: The head term is `primary` and appears verbatim in the title and H1 (9-3-2).
Variants belong in H2s, the FAQ and body copy — never stuffed, and never in the title.
A term appears in exactly one page's cluster, site-wide.
A variant is never another page's head term.
Entity-qualified variants belong to the entity page, never to the generic tool (the generic/entity rule, 9-4-1). `{state} paycheck calculator` is in the state page's cluster, not the paycheck tool's.

plannedPages.$comment: The 9 guides from spec section 6-2, declared before they are written. Their head terms are NOT yet measured, so they are exempt from the measured-target rule until promoted into `pages` — but they are NOT exempt from collision checks. A guide that duplicates a tool page's intent is cannibalisation that ships, and guides are the main external-link asset (9-5-2), so it would be the expensive kind.
plannedPages.promotionRule: A planned page becomes a real page only after its head term is measured and added to data/keywords.json, and its cluster passes every check in scripts/audit_seo.py.

platform.$comment: How the specification in this file reaches the pages, on Base44. The specification is authoritative; the dashboard is a rendering target (rule 3-7-6).
platform.name: Base44

entityFieldMapping.$comment: Each generated page is one row of a Base44 entity. These fields are populated from data/onpage.generated.json, never typed by hand — 51 hand-entered titles is 51 chances to drift from the formula.
entityFieldMapping.slug: the URL segment, from the dataset (rule 6-7-5)
entityFieldMapping.json_ld: onPage.jsonLd blocks for that template, resolved

rules: Nothing in the SEO panel is typed by hand for a generated page. It is imported from data/onpage.generated.json, which scripts/generate_onpage.py produces and scripts/audit_seo.py validates.
A value that disagrees with the generated file is drift, and the generated file wins (rule 3-7-6).
Re-run the generator after any dataset change, then re-import. The annual tax update (section 16) changes 51 titles' year and every bracket sentence.
Requirements R1-R9 (3-1) are verified against the live app by the protocol in 3-5 before this mapping is trusted.

contentBudget.$comment: The anti-doorway thresholds from spec section 6-10-4, enforced by scripts/validate_content.py. A token counts as boilerplate when it appears on 80% or more of a template's pages.
contentBudget.$variantNote: The body must naturally use at least this many of its page's cluster variants. The uniqueness rules push toward varied phrasing and nothing pushed back — the first four pilot bodies scored 46% unique while hitting 0 of 5 variants. Two is deliberately low: this is a floor against forgetting, not a density target, and the anti-repetition rules in docs/copywriting.md guard the other side.

plannedModes.$comment: Capabilities that belong inside an existing tool rather than on a page of their own. The precedent is job-offer comparison: measured at 30 searches a month, so it became a mode rather than a page (6-1). A mode adds no URL, no cannibalisation risk and no thin page.

modes.rationale: Structurally sound: the comparison engine is identical, Eurostat publishes comparative price levels at country level, and a site offering city-vs-city plus country pages but no country-vs-country has a gap users notice.
blockers: Zero measured search volume. Rule 18-1 forbids building for an unproven target, and this project has been wrong three times by assuming volume it had not checked (20-5).
Eurostat dataset does not exist yet.
Within one region only. A US metro cannot be compared to a European country — BEA and Eurostat use different bases, and presenting the arithmetic anyway would be a confident wrong answer (4-9-3).
modes.economicNote: Even with volume, international traffic carries materially lower AdSense RPM than US traffic, so a country comparison is worth less per visit than its search volume suggests. That does not make it wrong — it makes the threshold for building it higher, not lower.
modes.decision: Build as a THIRD MODE of the existing comparison tool, never as its own page, and only after: (1) the head keywords are measured into data/keywords.json, and (2) the Eurostat dataset exists. Until both, it stays here as a recorded decision rather than an open question.
keywordsToMeasure: cost of living comparison between countries

sitemaps.$comment: Section 6-8-6 described this segmentation in prose and shipped no artifact, so a builder had nothing to implement. Each page's segment is now derived by template and written into data/onpage.generated.json, and the index below is the file tree to produce. The point of segmenting is gate 1: one flat sitemap tells you '60% indexed' and not which template failed.
rules: Every indexable page appears in exactly one segment. A page in two segments is a page whose coverage number cannot be read.
A page is listed only when it is actually reachable and returns 200. A sitemap that lists a page the build has not produced teaches Search Console to distrust the file.
No page carrying a PENDING_ placeholder is listed, and none is linked from a directory either — it is not built at all until its data exists (rule 5-3).
lastmod comes from site.contentUpdated, the same declared date as schema.org dateModified. A lastmod taken from the build clock claims a change on every deploy and Google learns to ignore the field.
No priority and no changefreq. Google has ignored both for years and they are one more thing to keep consistent.
robots.txt names the index only; the index names the segments.
